title: CCDV-F Mock Exam #11 (Hard Tier)
description: Full-length 53-question high-difficulty simulation for Claude Certified Developer - Foundations (120 minutes). Elevated distractor plausibility and edge-case testing.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A trading-desk assistant streams responses from the Messages API. The HTTP response arrives with status 200, and the handler has already received `message_start`, one `content_block_start`, and several `text_delta` chunks when the stream delivers an `event: error` whose payload type is `overloaded_error`. The handler's retry classifier only inspects HTTP status codes, so it logs the call as a success and saves the partial text as the assistant turn. What is the correct handling?

options.text: Keep the partial text as the assistant turn and send a follow-up asking Claude to continue from where it stopped, since the 200 status shows the request was accepted and billed.
Classify the failure as terminal, because an error event arriving after a 200 status means the request body itself was invalid and will fail identically on any retry.
Treat the in-stream `overloaded_error` like an HTTP 529: discard the partial turn instead of committing it to history, then retry the whole request with backoff.
Keep reading until `message_delta` delivers a final `stop_reason`, since the error event is advisory and generation resumes automatically once capacity returns.

questions.explanation: Once a stream has opened, the HTTP status is already 200, so failures that occur mid-stream (such as `overloaded_error`, the streaming counterpart of a 529) arrive as an `error` event rather than as a status code. Only `message_stop` marks a complete message, so everything accumulated before the error is provisional. The correct path discards the partial turn and retries the retriable overload with backoff instead of trusting the status code or committing half a turn to history.

distractor_explanations.A: The stream never reached `message_stop`, so the accumulated turn is provisional. Committing it writes an incomplete message into history, which is exactly the failure the course warns about.
distractor_explanations.B: Invalid requests are rejected with a 400 before any stream opens. An overload is transient Anthropic-side load and belongs in the retriable bucket.
distractor_explanations.D: An error event terminates the stream; no `message_delta` or `message_stop` follows. Waiting leaves the handler hung on a dead connection.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A support agent streams responses with adaptive thinking enabled and tools registered. Its stream assembler handles `thinking_delta`, `text_delta`, and `input_json_delta` events and silently ignores any other delta type. Single-turn answers work, but every request that sends back a `tool_result` after a thinking-enabled tool call is rejected by the API. What is the most likely defect?

options.text: The assembler drops each thinking block's `signature_delta`, so the thinking block written back into history has no valid signature and fails verification.
The `tool_result` block must repeat the thinking text so the model can connect its earlier reasoning to the result, and the assembler never copies it across.
Adaptive thinking cannot be combined with tool use, so the API rejects any tool round-trip once thinking is on; the fix is to disable thinking for agentic calls.
The assembler should strip thinking blocks from the assistant turn before appending it, because a thinking block is only valid inside the response that originally produced it.

questions.explanation: In a streamed response, each thinking block's signature arrives as a `signature_delta` just before the block closes. Thinking blocks must go back to the API exactly as they arrived, signature included; the signature is what proves the reasoning was not altered. An assembler that ignores unrecognized delta types silently strips the signature, and the failure only surfaces on the next tool-use turn.

distractor_explanations.B: A `tool_result` carries the `tool_use_id` and the result content; it never repeats reasoning. The defect is in the assistant turn's thinking block.
distractor_explanations.C: Thinking and tool use combine; the course recommends thinking for agentic planning loops, subject to the carry-back rule.
distractor_explanations.D: In a tool-use loop, thinking blocks must be passed back unchanged. Removing them is itself a cause of rejection, not the fix.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A nightly Message Batches job submits 80,000 requests, each with a `custom_id` equal to the source record's primary key. When the batch ends, the results show most entries with result type `succeeded`, about 1,200 `errored`, and about 300 `expired`. What is the correct follow-up?

options.text: Resubmit all 80,000 requests, because a batch is atomic: once any request inside it fails, the service discards the partial results and bills only for completed batches.
Poll the same batch again after a few hours, because expired requests are automatically re-queued by the service and will move to succeeded once capacity frees up.
Resubmit the final 1,500 requests in submission order, because errored and expired requests are always the ones still queued at the tail of the input file when the window closes.
Join results to inputs by `custom_id`, inspect why the errored requests failed, and put only the errored and expired requests into a new batch for resubmission.

questions.explanation: Each request in a batch is processed independently, and its result is reported on its own as succeeded, errored, canceled, or expired. Results come back in arbitrary order, so `custom_id` is the only reliable join key. Expired requests were never processed within the 24-hour window, and errored requests should be inspected first, because a malformed request will fail again. The fix is a targeted resubmission, not a rerun of the whole job.

distractor_explanations.A: Batch requests are processed and reported independently. Succeeded results are valid, and resubmitting them doubles the cost.
distractor_explanations.B: Expired means the request was not processed within the batch's 24-hour window. It is not retried for you and must go into a new batch.
distractor_explanations.C: Results return in arbitrary order and failures are not positional. Only `custom_id` identifies which inputs need another attempt.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A claims platform built on the first-party API uploads each policy PDF once through the Files API and references its `file_id` in every request. The customer now requires the workload to run on Google Vertex AI. What must change in the request-building code?

options.text: Replace the `file_id` references: the Files API beta is not available on Vertex AI or Bedrock, so send the PDF another way, such as a base64 `document` block.
Re-upload each PDF through the Files API using Google Cloud credentials so new Vertex-scoped `file_id` values replace the first-party ones, then update the references.
Rasterize each PDF into page images, because `document` blocks are a first-party-only feature and Vertex AI accepts only image content blocks for visual input.
Nothing in the content blocks changes; only the client class and credentials change, because Vertex AI exposes the same request surface as the first-party API, Files API included.

questions.explanation: The Files API (upload once, then reference a `file_id`) is in beta and, per the course, is not available on Bedrock or Vertex AI. Moving the workload to Vertex therefore breaks every `file_id` reference, and the code must fall back to sending the content itself, for example as a base64 `document` block. A platform migration has to check feature parity, not just client configuration.

distractor_explanations.B: There is no Files API on Vertex AI to upload into. First-party `file_id` values do not transfer and cannot be created there.
distractor_explanations.C: The unavailable piece is the Files API reference, not the document block. Sending the PDF itself, such as base64 in a document block, is the portable route.
distractor_explanations.D: Feature availability differs by platform. The course notes that the Files API beta is not available on Bedrock or Vertex AI.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A multi-tenant extraction service builds a different JSON schema for every request from each tenant's custom field definitions, and passes it as `output_config.format` with type `json_schema`. Latency is consistently higher than in a fixed-schema pilot, and input token counts are slightly higher than the prompt alone should produce. Which TWO statements explain these observations? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Each new schema is compiled into a grammar before output can be constrained; grammars are cached for reuse, so per-request schemas keep paying compile latency.
Constrained decoding checks the finished response against the schema and silently regenerates it on failure, so the extra latency comes from hidden retry passes on the server.
Structured outputs add an injected system prompt that describes the expected format, and those extra tokens are billed as ordinary input tokens on every request.
The schema is re-tokenized and counted as output tokens on every request, which is why each response takes longer to finish and why token counts drift upward.
Any request carrying `output_config.format` is routed to a slower decoding tier, so latency rises by a fixed amount whether or not that schema has been seen before.

questions.explanation: Structured outputs have two documented costs. The first request on a new schema is slower because the API compiles the schema into a grammar; compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use, so stable schemas pay once while constantly changing schemas pay over and over. Enabling the feature also adds an injected system prompt describing the format, and those tokens are billed as input. Per-request schemas explain both observations.

distractor_explanations.B: Constrained decoding restricts which tokens can be generated as the response is produced. It does not generate, validate, and retry.
distractor_explanations.D: The overhead is an injected system prompt billed as input. Output length depends on the response, not on the schema.
distractor_explanations.E: The latency cost is tied to compiling a new schema. A stable schema pays it once and then reuses the cached grammar.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: During a regional traffic spike, a service's dashboard shows a surge of HTTP 529 responses from the Anthropic API while the service's own request rate is well under its documented limits. The engineering manager proposes requesting a higher rate-limit tier to stop the errors. What is the most accurate assessment?

options.text: A 529 signals that the account's per-minute token budget is exhausted, so moving to a higher rate-limit tier is the right long-term fix while backoff covers the short term.
A 529 indicates malformed or oversized request bodies that some clients produce under load, so it should be classified as terminal and the failing payloads inspected.
A 529 means Anthropic's service is temporarily overloaded, not that the account hit its limits; a higher tier won't help, so back off and degrade gracefully if it persists.
A 529 means the client's SDK retries are colliding under load and amplifying traffic, so disabling SDK retries will remove the errors at their source.

questions.explanation: In the course's taxonomy, a 429 is a rate limit and a 529 means the service is temporarily overloaded. Both are retriable, but a 529 reflects load on Anthropic's side rather than the caller's quota, so raising the account's limits does nothing. The decision table prescribes backoff for a 529, then a fallback path or a graceful error if it persists.

distractor_explanations.A: That describes a 429 rate limit. The course separates 529 (overload) from rate-limit signals.
distractor_explanations.B: Malformed requests return a terminal 400. A 529 is transient, server-side load and is retriable.
distractor_explanations.D: Retry configuration does not cause overload responses. Disabling retries only turns transient overloads into hard failures.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A team wraps every `client.messages.create` call in a decorator that retries up to 5 times with exponential backoff on any exception. The Anthropic SDK client is left at its default settings. During a burst of 429s, logs show many more attempts per logical request than the decorator should allow, and recovery is slower than expected. What is the best fix?

options.text: Restrict the decorator to connection errors only, because the SDK never retries 429 responses itself, so rate limits must stay with application-level retry logic.
Decide where retries live: the SDK already retries transient failures, so a second layer multiplies attempts. Rely on the SDK, or turn its retries down and own the path.
Raise the decorator's cap to 10 attempts so it outlasts the SDK's own retries, since the outermost retry layer should always hold the largest budget in the call stack.
Remove the decorator's backoff and retry immediately, since the SDK's internal backoff already spaces the calls and an outer delay only adds latency on top of it.

questions.explanation: The Anthropic client libraries automatically retry transient failures with progressive delays, up to a configurable number of attempts. Wrapping them in an application retry loop multiplies the attempts (outer attempts × SDK attempts) instead of capping them, which deepens a rate limit. The course's rule is to decide where retries live and never let two layers retry the same failure without knowing about each other.

distractor_explanations.A: The SDK does retry transient failures, including rate limits. This change rests on a false premise and keeps two layers retrying other errors.
distractor_explanations.C: A larger outer cap makes the multiplication worse. The problem is two uncoordinated retry layers, not an undersized cap.
distractor_explanations.D: Immediate outer retries count against the same limit and deepen it. The course warns that instant retries make rate limits worse.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A developer sends a signed contract to the Messages API as base64 and receives a 400 validation error. Which content block is correctly structured for a PDF?

options.text: `{"type": "image", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": "<b64>"}, "title": "msa.pdf"}`
`{"type": "file", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": "<b64>"}, "filename": "signed-msa.pdf"}`
`{"type": "document", "name": "msa.pdf", "source": {"type": "pdf", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": "<b64>"}}`
`{"type": "document", "source": {"type": "base64", "media_type": "application/pdf", "data": "<b64>"}, "title": "msa.pdf"}`

questions.explanation: PDFs are sent in a `document` block, whose `source` follows the same pattern as images: base64 with a `media_type` of `application/pdf`, a URL, or a Files API `file_id`. A document block has no required `name` field. `title` (a readable name) and `context` (extra metadata) are optional.

distractor_explanations.A: PDFs are sent in a document block, not an image block, even though the source structure looks the same.
distractor_explanations.B: There is no file content block type. PDFs use the document type, with an optional `title` rather than a `filename`.
distractor_explanations.C: Inline bytes use a source of type base64, not pdf, and `name` is not a document block field; the optional readable name is `title`.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A customer has called Claude for two years through Amazon Bedrock's `InvokeModel` API with ARN-versioned model identifiers. Their new agent code is written against the Messages API and relies on broad feature parity with the first-party API. Inference and data must stay inside their configured AWS boundary. Which integration and model reference fit?

options.text: Claude in Amazon Bedrock: the Messages API at `/anthropic/v1/messages` with broad parity, data inside the AWS boundary, pinned by the `anthropic.`-prefixed model ID.
Claude Platform on AWS, because it is billed through the customer's AWS account and uses Anthropic's own model IDs and lifecycle, giving the closest parity with the first-party API.
Claude on Amazon Bedrock (legacy) through `Converse`, since `Converse` is Bedrock's Messages-compatible interface and the recommended route for new agent code on AWS.
Claude in Amazon Bedrock, pinned with the same model ID string the first-party API uses (for example `claude-opus-4-8`) so the agent code ports without changes.

questions.explanation: The course separates three AWS routes. Claude in Amazon Bedrock offers the Messages API at `/anthropic/v1/messages` with broad feature parity, keeps data inside the customer's AWS boundary, and pins with the `anthropic.` prefix format. Claude on Amazon Bedrock (legacy) uses InvokeModel/Converse with ARN-versioned identifiers. Claude Platform on AWS uses Anthropic model IDs, but inference runs outside the AWS boundary.

distractor_explanations.B: Claude Platform on AWS runs inference on Anthropic-operated infrastructure outside the AWS boundary, which breaks the stated residency constraint.
distractor_explanations.C: `Converse` and `InvokeModel` are the legacy integration with ARN-versioned identifiers. The Messages API integration is Claude in Amazon Bedrock.
distractor_explanations.D: Using Anthropic's own ID format is how Claude Platform on AWS pins models. Claude in Amazon Bedrock pins the `anthropic.`-prefixed full model ID.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A regulated EU insurer has standardized on Microsoft Foundry and wants two Claude models there: one listed as Hosted on Azure and one listed as Hosted on Anthropic. Their requirement is that inference stays on EU infrastructure under their Azure agreement. What should the developer conclude?

options.text: Both models qualify, because any Claude model consumed through Foundry inherits the customer's Azure data-residency terms regardless of where its inference actually runs.
Judge residency per model: the Azure-hosted model runs inference end to end on Azure; the Anthropic-hosted one does not meet EU residency. Confirm the split with Microsoft.
Neither model qualifies, because Claude on any third-party platform always runs on Anthropic infrastructure, so the insurer must move the workload to Bedrock or Vertex AI.
Both qualify as long as the Foundry resource is created in an EU region, because the resource's region pins the inference location for every model it hosts.

questions.explanation: Microsoft Foundry offers Claude in two hosting forms. Hosted on Azure models run inference end to end on Azure infrastructure. Hosted on Anthropic models run on Anthropic-operated infrastructure and do not satisfy EU regional residency. Residency assumptions therefore depend on the hosting form of each specific model, and the course says to confirm the current split with Microsoft before committing a regulated workload.

distractor_explanations.A: Foundry hosting is set per model, and Anthropic-hosted Foundry models do not run inference on Azure infrastructure.
distractor_explanations.C: Hosted-on-Azure models run inference end to end on Azure, so rejecting both is wrong.
distractor_explanations.D: The resource region does not override a model's hosting form; Anthropic-hosted models still fail EU regional residency.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A federal contractor must run a Claude workload at FedRAMP High, and procurement has shortlisted five routes. Which TWO are authorized routes according to the course? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Claude for Government (C4G), which holds a direct FedRAMP High authorization through Palantir Federal Cloud Service – Supporting Services.
Claude via Amazon Bedrock GovCloud, which is approved for FedRAMP High and DoD IL4/5 workloads run by US federal agencies.
The first-party Claude API under a Zero Data Retention agreement, since ZDR takes stored data out of the authorization's scope.
Claude Enterprise bought through AWS Marketplace, since it is provisioned and billed inside the agency's existing AWS account and inherits its controls.
Claude Platform on AWS in a US region, since inference billed through AWS inherits the account's FedRAMP authorization.

questions.explanation: The course lists three authorized routes as of publication: Claude for Government (C4G), with a direct FedRAMP High authorization through Palantir FedCloud (PFCS-SS); Claude via Amazon Bedrock GovCloud, approved for FedRAMP High and DoD IL4/5; and Claude via Vertex AI Assured Workloads. Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace is explicitly not FedRAMP authorized. Teams should verify current status at trust.anthropic.com before configuring anything.

distractor_explanations.C: ZDR is a retention arrangement, not a FedRAMP authorization. The commercial endpoint is not an authorized route.
distractor_explanations.D: The course states that Claude Enterprise on AWS Marketplace is not FedRAMP authorized.
distractor_explanations.E: Claude Platform on AWS runs inference on Anthropic-operated infrastructure outside the AWS boundary, and it is not listed as an authorized route.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A release reviewer audits model references in three services: Service X uses `"sonnet"`, Service Y uses `"claude-haiku-4-5"`, and Service Z uses `"claude-haiku-4-5-20251001"`. Policy says no service may use a reference that can resolve to a new snapshot without a code change. Under the course's versioning guidance, which services violate the policy?

options.text: Only X, because an identifier that names both a model family and a version number, such as `claude-haiku-4-5`, already resolves to one fixed snapshot.
X and Y: `sonnet` is an alias, and `claude-haiku-4-5` is a pre-4.6 ID without its date suffix, so it can move. Z is a pinned snapshot.
All three, because pinning is configured in the platform console rather than in the model string, so every string reference tracks the latest snapshot.
Only Z, because date-suffixed identifiers refer to retired snapshots that the API silently redirects to the family's current version.

questions.explanation: Aliases such as `opus` or `sonnet` move over time and can resolve to different versions on different platforms. For models before 4.6, a pinned reference needs the ID plus a date suffix (for example `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`). For Claude 4.6 and later, the model ID alone pins a snapshot. Pinning makes an upstream model update a deliberate change rather than a silent one. Confirm the current convention at build time.

distractor_explanations.A: For models before 4.6, pinning requires the date suffix. Without it, the identifier behaves as an alias.
distractor_explanations.C: A pinned full model ID in the request is what fixes the snapshot. The course shows the date-suffixed ID as the pinned form.
distractor_explanations.D: For pre-4.6 models the date-suffixed ID is the pinned form, which is exactly the course's example of fixing the version.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A law firm's application calls the first-party Claude API from inside its own environment, authenticated through SSO via a firm-approved LLM gateway. For privilege audits, compliance asks where the record of prompts, responses, and tool-call payloads will come from. What is the accurate answer?

options.text: A PostToolUse hook in the firm's Claude Code settings captures the full conversation, including prompts and responses from the application's own API calls.
Anthropic's compliance tooling records prompts, responses, and tool payloads for every direct API request, so the firm only needs to request a periodic export for audits.
The application must log conversations itself and route them to an approved destination; Anthropic does not capture that content by default on direct API traffic.
Turning on Zero Data Retention produces an auditable retention record for each request, which gives compliance the per-request evidence that privilege audits require.

questions.explanation: For attorney-client privilege, the course's surviving pattern is direct API calls from the firm's own application, authenticated via SSO and routed through an approved gateway with full request and response logging. It specifically notes that Compliance Conversation content (prompts, responses, and tool call payloads) is not captured by Anthropic by default on direct API traffic, so the organization must log it in the application layer and send it to an approved destination.

distractor_explanations.A: Claude Code hooks govern Claude Code sessions. They do not record traffic from a separate application calling the API.
distractor_explanations.B: The course states that this conversation content is not captured by Anthropic by default on direct API traffic.
distractor_explanations.D: ZDR minimizes what is retained; it does not produce the firm's audit record. Logging belongs in the application layer.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A digital-health startup has a BAA with Anthropic covering a dedicated HIPAA-enabled organization. To move fast, the team plans to (1) iterate on prompts containing PHI in the Console Workbench and (2) upload patient PDFs once through the Files API beta and reference them by `file_id` in production. What should the developer flag?

options.text: Only the Workbench step, because the Files API is part of the core API surface and is covered automatically once the organization has been HIPAA-enabled.
Both: the BAA does not cover Console or Workbench use, and it does not cover beta features such as the Files API, so PHI must stay on covered API features.
Neither, because once the organization is HIPAA-enabled the BAA extends to every surface that organization can reach, Console and beta endpoints included.
Only the Files API step, because the Workbench runs inside the HIPAA-enabled organization, so any PHI entered there falls under the same BAA coverage.

questions.explanation: Anthropic arranges first-party BAA coverage through a dedicated HIPAA-enabled organization, but the course is explicit that the BAA does not cover Console, Workbench, beta features, or consumer plans, and that not all API features are covered. PHI workflows therefore have to avoid both the Workbench and beta features like the Files API unless current eligibility documentation says otherwise.

distractor_explanations.A: The BAA excludes beta features, and the Files API is in beta.
distractor_explanations.C: The BAA's scope is not "everything the organization can reach." Console, Workbench, and beta features are explicitly excluded, so the developer must verify eligibility per feature.
distractor_explanations.D: The course explicitly lists Console and Workbench as outside BAA coverage.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: During a customer engagement, a developer fixes a pagination bug in a widely used open-source MCP server and also writes a general retry helper around it. They want to contribute the fix. Which plan matches the course's contribution guidance?

options.text: Open the PR right away with the fix and a test, and raise licensing with the customer only if the maintainer asks about provenance during the review.
Open a PR on the server's repository with the fix, the retry helper, and a refactor of the pagination module, so maintainers can see the full context of the improvement.
Clear the right to contribute the engagement code, then open a focused PR on the server's own repository with only the fix, an example, a test, and stated assumptions.
Submit the fix and the retry helper together to the Claude Cookbook as one example, since the Cookbook is the central channel for contributions to the Claude ecosystem.

questions.explanation: Contributions go through the channel built for their shape: open-source MCP servers and tools have their own repositories, while the Cookbook takes focused reference examples. Maintainers accept what they can verify: code that does one thing, an example that shows it running, a test that proves it, and a statement of assumptions. Licensing and attribution for engagement code are a gate that comes before any technical review.

distractor_explanations.A: Rights and attribution come before technical review. An engagement licensing constraint can block the merge regardless of code quality.
distractor_explanations.B: A sprawling contribution forces the reviewer to reconstruct intent. The code should do one thing.
distractor_explanations.D: The Cookbook is for focused reference implementations. A fix to an MCP server belongs in that server's own repository, and bundling the helper makes the change harder to verify.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A service-account credential for an internal ticketing API is used by four services and two CI pipelines. Security wants a design that limits exposure and makes rotation cheap. Which TWO practices does the course recommend? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Store the credential in each service's `.claude/settings.local.json`, because that file is git-ignored and therefore keeps the value out of repository history entirely.
Rotate only when the credential expires or a consumer reports a 401, because unscheduled rotations break the consumers that have the value hardcoded.
Scope the credential narrowly and keep a record of which services use it, so a leak reaches less and rotation surfaces no forgotten consumers.
Keep the credential in a managed secret store that serves it to authorized callers at runtime and records reads, so one rotation reaches every consumer.
Base64-encode the credential inside each service's committed configuration file so the raw value is never readable in plain text during code review.

questions.explanation: The course's three practices are separation, storage, and rotation: keep values out of the configuration that references them; use a secret store when a credential is shared or must be audited, so one rotation reaches every consumer; and rotate on a schedule and after suspected exposure. Two habits make rotation cheaper: scope each credential narrowly, and keep a record of which services use it.

distractor_explanations.A: A per-machine settings file still stores the secret on disk and multiplies the copies. The course puts shared secrets in a secret store and keeps them out of configuration files.
distractor_explanations.B: Rotate on a schedule and immediately after any suspected exposure. Consumers that read the value by reference rotate without code changes.
distractor_explanations.E: Encoding is not protection. A committed value lives in history and must be treated as compromised.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Hard Tier)
questions.prompt: A product team runs a long-lived agent on Claude Managed Agents and references it by agent ID across many sessions. They want new sessions to use an updated compliance-review skill, so a developer adds the skill to the payload that starts each session. New sessions do not use it. What is the correct change?

options.text: Update the agent definition itself, because Managed Agents attach skills when the versioned agent resource is defined, not when a session starts.
Commit the SKILL.md to the repository's `.claude/skills` directory, so the managed sandbox discovers it from the filesystem when each new session starts.
Set `settingSources` to include `project` in the session configuration so the hosted loop loads skills from the project's filesystem sources.
Send the `code-execution-2025-08-25` and `skills-2025-10-02` beta headers with the session request, which is what turns on per-session skills.

questions.explanation: With Claude Managed Agents, you define the agent once as an API resource that names the model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers, and skills, and Anthropic loads the skill server-side when the agent runs. The course states that skills are attached when the agent resource is defined, not at session time, and that you change which skills are available by updating the agent definition.

distractor_explanations.B: Managed Agents load skills server-side from the agent resource. There is no filesystem discovery step on the caller's side.
distractor_explanations.C: `settingSources` is an Agent SDK setting that controls filesystem loading in your own process. It does not apply to an Anthropic-hosted agent resource.
distractor_explanations.D: Those headers belong to the Messages API skills path. Managed Agents attach skills in the agent definition.
